title: House shelves Hegseth impeachment effort in 211-204 vote
excerpt: The House voted 211-204 on Tuesday to send eight articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to the Judiciary Committee, effectively halting the effort for this Congress.
content:
The House of Representatives voted 211 to 204 on Tuesday, Nov. 10, to send eight articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to the House Judiciary Committee — a procedural move that effectively halts the effort for the remainder of this Congress.

Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, a Republican, reintroduced the articles on Monday, accusing Hegseth of high crimes and misdemeanors tied to the war with Iran and U.S. strikes on suspected drug boats in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific. Massie was the only Republican to vote against sending the articles to committee. All 203 Democrats who voted also opposed the referral, seeking a floor vote. Voting to refer were 210 Republicans and independent Rep. Kevin Kiley of California. Eighteen members did not vote — 11 Democrats, including former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, and seven Republicans.

The House never voted on the charges themselves. Three of the eight articles concern the Iran war, which the Pentagon says has cost $47.1 billion through Oct. 16. The articles also accuse Hegseth of ordering extrajudicial killings of suspected militants and ignoring laws meant to protect civilians in conflict zones. Hegseth rejected the allegations at a Pentagon briefing earlier Tuesday.

The referral does not require the Judiciary Committee to act, and with the current Congress ending Jan. 3, 2027, the articles are expected to expire without a vote on their merits. Massie said he will not file another resolution and leaves Congress in early January. But the question may return: Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate in the Nov. 3 midterm elections and take the majorities in January, when they could revive proceedings.

In a separate vote Tuesday, House Republicans elected Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio as their new minority leader.

For Webb County readers, the practical effect is timing. Nothing changes before January, when the new Congress takes its seats — including reelected Rep. Henry Cuellar of Texas' 28th District. Webb Watch will track whether the new majority revisits the impeachment question once it is seated.

Sources: Reuters, Nov. 11, 2026; NPR, Nov. 11, 2026; CBS News; The Hill.
